html_source:
In brief

Parody. "They believe in rod, the scourger almighty, creator of hell upon earth [...] whence he shall come to drudge for a living and be paid": after the Citizen vituperates the brutal punishment regimes on British warships, this mocking sentence amplifies what he has said in language that apes the Apostles' Creed. Two parodies earlier, mock-heroic glorification of the Citizen was balanced against humorous disdain for his enemies. Here Joyce takes aim only at the English, and at the absurdities of Christian belief.

At more length

The Apostles' Creed begins, "I believe in God, the Father Almighty, Creator of heaven and earth." The British authorities, on the other hand, "believe in rod, the scourger almighty, creator of hell upon earth." Replacing God with rod (the "long cane" mentioned by the Citizen, which was used mainly on young boys) is linguistically clever and also makes some analogical sense, since from the beginning Christians understood their god as a scourger of sin who sends the unrighteous to an eternity of torment in hell. The creed only mentions hell some lines later, when the Son descends into it, but the British have created it right here on earth. 

The Christian creed continues, "and in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary." Joyce's says instead, "and in Jacky Tar, the son of a gun, who was conceived of unholy boast, born of the fighting navy." Jack Tar was a proverbial English name for sailors in the navy or the merchant marine, inspired by their practice of slicking themselves down with tar for protection against ropes and seaspray. The "unholy boast" (echoing "Holy Ghost" rather than "Holy Spirit") possibly refers to some disreputable transient's boast of having fathered a son on some girl. After entering biological existence the son is born a second time in His Majesty's Navy, just as Jesus Christ was first spiritually conceived as the Son of God and then physically incarnated in the womb of Mary.

Our Savior "suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into hell; the third day He rose again from the dead." Our Jack's course was rather different: he "suffered under rump and dozen, was scarified, flayed and curried, yelled like bloody hell, the third day he arose again from the bed." The old Irish phrase "rump and dozen" (Green's Dictionary of Slang finds it used as early as 1786) seems originally to have referred to a wager or a feast—the loser of a bet would give the winner a rump of beef and a dozen bottles of claret—but that meaning is inapplicable here. An 1832 British satirical print suggests that another sense having to do with corporal punishment had become current. It shows multiple lashes (a dozen?) being administered to a royal rump bearing the tattoed image of an anchor. In fact the Citizen has alluded to this naval meaning: "A rump and dozen [...] was what that old ruffian sir John Beresford called it but the modern God's Englishman calls it caning on the breech." After being thus "scarified, flayed, and curried," in the British Navy's halfway approximation of a crucifixion (its full monty was keelhauling), Jack Tar takes to his bed for three miserable days of recuperation.

After arising from the dead, Jesus Christ "ascended into heavens, sitteth at the right hand of God, the Father Almighty. From thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead." Jack Tar, after he got up from his bed, "steered into haven, sitteth on his beamend till further orders whence he shall come to drudge for a living and be paid." Unlike Jesus, there is no glorious ending for this guy who has been through hell. He simply continues to drudge for a living, confirming the Citizen's view that the British Empire is built on "drudges and whipped serfs."

Bloom mounts a real challenge to this view, asking "isn't discipline the same everywhere," but the parody does not seem to skewer the xenophobic portrait so much as humorously restate it. After saying that the empire is built on the backs of serfs the Citizen observes, "And the tragedy of it is, [...] they believe it. The unfortunate yahoos believe it." The parody turns this belief in submission into a creed: "They believe in rod, the scourger almighty...."

In addition to expressing dislike for the English social structure, the parody also seems intended to undermine the foundational document of Christianity. Stephen makes a mockery of the Apostles' Creed in Scylla and Charybdis and is celebrated for doing so in Oxen of the Sun: "Parson Steve, apostates' creed!" The same paragraph of Oxen shows him mocking the British Beatitudes: "Beer, beef, business, bibles, bulldogs, battleships, buggery and bishops." Church and State are equally oppressors of the human spirit—"two masters," as he calls them in Telemachus.

One particular point of convergence between imperial and clerical hierarchy should be noted in conclusion. The Citizen has observed that not only crew and officers assemble on the deck of a warship to witness the punishment of transgression, but also "the parson with his protestant bible." Catholics do not own bibles, because their church has judged them incapable of properly weighing the contents except via clerical instruction—one version of religious mind-control. Protestants do own them, but in the British navy the Good Book is thoroughly subordinated to the hierarchical discipline of the service. Patrick O'Brian's sea novels make this conjunction hilariously but chillingly clear in their descriptions of Sunday services, which are conducted exclusively by the Captain, their religious messages interwoven with detailed listings of naval crimes and their punishments. Nearly every transgression, sailors are reminded in these services, is punishable by death.

John Hunt 2026
